claim: Lateral habenula is believed to encode negative motivational stimuli and plays key roles in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders.
source: Lateral habenula is believed to encode negative motivational stimuli and plays key roles in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about established understanding in the field, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Transient activity in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) within the habenula is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
source: Transient activity in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) within the habenula and prefrontal cortical regions, as well as the coupling between these structures, is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transient activity in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) within prefrontal cortical regions is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
source: Transient activity in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) within the habenula and prefrontal cortical regions, as well as the coupling between these structures, is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MEG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coupling between habenula and prefrontal cortical regions in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
source: Transient activity in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) within the habenula and prefrontal cortical regions, as well as the coupling between these structures, is increased during the perception and processing of negative emotional stimuli compared to positive emotional stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by coherence analysis between LFP and MEG data.

claim: The increase in theta/alpha band synchronization in the frontal cortex-habenula network correlated with the emotional valence of the stimuli.
source: The increase in theta/alpha band synchronization in the frontal cortex-habenula network correlated with the emotional valence but not the arousal score of the stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in theta/alpha band synchronization in the frontal cortex-habenula network did not correlate with the arousal score of the stimuli.
source: The increase in theta/alpha band synchronization in the frontal cortex-habenula network correlated with the emotional valence but not the arousal score of the stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling results showing no significant effect of arousal.

claim: The habenula functionally links the forebrain with the midbrain structures that are involved in the release of dopamine (i.e., the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area).
source: The habenula is an epithalamic structure that functionally links the forebrain with the midbrain structures that are involved in the release of dopamine (i.e., the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area) and serotonin (i.e., raphe nucleus) (Wang and Aghajanian, 1977; Herkenham and Nauta, 1979; Hikosaka et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2011; Proulx et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The habenula functionally links the forebrain with the midbrain structures that are involved in the release of serotonin (i.e., raphe nucleus).
source: The habenula is an epithalamic structure that functionally links the forebrain with the midbrain structures that are involved in the release of dopamine (i.e., the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area) and serotonin (i.e., raphe nucleus) (Wang and Aghajanian, 1977; Herkenham and Nauta, 1979; Hikosaka et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2011; Proulx et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Activities in lateral habenula (LHb) increased during the processing of aversive events such as omission of predicted rewards.
source: Animal studies showed that activities in lateral habenula (LHb) increased during the processing of aversive events such as omission of predicted rewards, and stimuli provoking anxiety, stress, pain and fear (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Hikosaka, 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Activities in lateral habenula (LHb) increased during the processing of stimuli provoking anxiety, stress, pain and fear.
source: Animal studies showed that activities in lateral habenula (LHb) increased during the processing of aversive events such as omission of predicted rewards, and stimuli provoking anxiety, stress, pain and fear (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Hikosaka, 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Hyperexcitability and dysfunction of the LHb have been implicated in the development of psychiatric disorders including depressive disorder and bipolar disorders.
source: Hyperexcitability and dysfunction of the LHb have been implicated in the development of psychiatric disorders including depressive disorder and bipolar disorders (Fakhoury, 2017; Yang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In rodents, LHb firing rate and metabolism is elevated in parallel with depressive-like phenotypes such as reduction in locomotor and rearing behaviors.
source: In rodents, LHb firing rate and metabolism is elevated in parallel with depressive-like phenotypes such as reduction in locomotor and rearing behaviors (Caldecott-Hazard et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent study.

claim: Habenula activities increase during acquisition and recall of conditioned fear.
source: Habenula activities also increase during acquisition and recall of conditioned fear (González-Pardo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging has revealed smaller habenula volume in patients with depressive and bipolar disorders.
source: In human participants, high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging has revealed smaller habenula volume in patients with depressive and bipolar disorders (Savitz et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an MRI study.

claim: Dysfunction of the LHb has been involved in schizophrenia.
source: Dysfunction of the LHb has also been involved in different cognitive disorders, such as schizophrenia (Shepard et al., 2006) and addiction (Velasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dysfunction of the LHb has been involved in addiction.
source: Dysfunction of the LHb has also been involved in different cognitive disorders, such as schizophrenia (Shepard et al., 2006) and addiction (Velasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the LHb has potential therapeutic effects in treatment-resistant depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia.
source: More direct evidence of the involvement of the LHb in psychiatric disorders in humans comes from deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the LHb that has potential therapeutic effects in treatment-resistant depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia (Sartorius et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DBS studies.

claim: Dysfunction and dysregulation of emotion-related brain circuits may precipitate mood disorders.
source: Dysfunction and dysregulation of emotion-related brain circuits may precipitate mood disorders (Phillips et al., 2003b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During the depression-like state in rodents, LHb neuron firing increased with the mean firing rate at the theta band.
source: Previous studies on rodent models of depression showed that, during the depression-like state in rodents, LHb neuron firing increased with the mean firing rate at the theta band (Li et al., 2011) and LHb neurons fire in bursts and phase locked to local theta band field potentials (Yang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent study.

claim: LHb neurons fire in bursts and phase locked to local theta band field potentials during the depression-like state in rodents.
source: Previous studies on rodent models of depression showed that, during the depression-like state in rodents, LHb neuron firing increased with the mean firing rate at the theta band (Li et al., 2011) and LHb neurons fire in bursts and phase locked to local theta band field potentials (Yang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent study.

claim: 13 out of the 18 recorded habenula during rest showed power of oscillatory activities peaking in the theta/alpha frequency range (5–10 Hz).
source: We detected the power of oscillatory activities peaking in the theta/alpha frequency range (here defined as 5–10 Hz) in 13 out of the 18 recorded habenula during rest compared to 7 of the 18 recorded habenula with peaks in beta band (12–30 Hz) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis using the FOOOF algorithm on resting LFP recordings.

claim: 7 of the 18 recorded habenula during rest showed power of oscillatory activities peaking in beta band (12–30 Hz).
source: We detected the power of oscillatory activities peaking in the theta/alpha frequency range (here defined as 5–10 Hz) in 13 out of the 18 recorded habenula during rest compared to 7 of the 18 recorded habenula with peaks in beta band (12–30 Hz) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis using the FOOOF algorithm on resting LFP recordings.

claim: The average peak frequency for theta/alpha oscillations in the habenula during rest was 8.2 ± 1.1 Hz (ranges from 6.1 Hz to 10 Hz).
source: The average peak frequency was 8.2 ± 1.1 Hz (ranges from 6.1 Hz to 10 Hz) for theta/alpha, and 15.1 ± 1.8 Hz (ranges from 12.5 Hz to 16.9 Hz) for beta band (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of resting LFP data.

claim: The average peak frequency for beta oscillations in the habenula during rest was 15.1 ± 1.8 Hz (ranges from 12.5 Hz to 16.9 Hz).
source: The average peak frequency was 8.2 ± 1.1 Hz (ranges from 6.1 Hz to 10 Hz) for theta/alpha, and 15.1 ± 1.8 Hz (ranges from 12.5 Hz to 16.9 Hz) for beta band (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of resting LFP data.

claim: 3 out of the 18 recorded habenula showed oscillatory activities in both theta/alpha and beta bands during rest.
source: 3 out of the 18 recorded habenula showed oscillatory activities in both theta/alpha and beta bands.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of resting LFP recordings.

claim: The power spectra normalized to the baseline activity showed a significant event-related synchronization (ERS) in the habenula spanning across 2–30 Hz from 50 to 800 ms after the presentation of all stimuli.
source: The power spectra normalized to the baseline activity (−2000 to −200 ms) showed a significant event-related synchronization (ERS) in the habenula spanning across 2–30 Hz from 50 to 800 ms after the presentation of all stimuli (pcluster < 0.05, Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-frequency analysis of LFP data with statistical testing.

claim: There is a cluster with significant difference in the theta/alpha range (5–10 Hz) at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms) after stimulus presentation between negative and positive emotional pictures.
source: Permutation tests were applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects. This identified two clusters with significant difference for the two emotional valence conditions: one in the theta/alpha range (5–10 Hz) at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms, Figure 3D, E) after stimulus presentation and another in the theta range (4–7 Hz) at a longer latency (from 2700 to 3300 ms, Figure 3D, F), with higher increase in the identified frequency bands with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in both clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation tests on LFP power spectra.

claim: There is a cluster with significant difference in the theta range (4–7 Hz) at a longer latency (from 2700 to 3300 ms) after stimulus presentation between negative and positive emotional pictures.
source: Permutation tests were applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects. This identified two clusters with significant difference for the two emotional valence conditions: one in the theta/alpha range (5–10 Hz) at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms, Figure 3D, E) after stimulus presentation and another in the theta range (4–7 Hz) at a longer latency (from 2700 to 3300 ms, Figure 3D, F), with higher increase in the identified frequency bands with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in both clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation tests on LFP power spectra.

claim: Higher increase in theta/alpha (5–10 Hz) power at 100-500 ms was observed with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in the habenula.
source: Permutation tests were applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects. This identified two clusters with significant difference for the two emotional valence conditions: one in the theta/alpha range (5–10 Hz) at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms, Figure 3D, E) after stimulus presentation and another in the theta range (4–7 Hz) at a longer latency (from 2700 to 3300 ms, Figure 3D, F), with higher increase in the identified frequency bands with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in both clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation tests on LFP power spectra.

claim: Higher increase in theta (4–7 Hz) power at 2700-3300 ms was observed with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in the habenula.
source: Permutation tests were applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects. This identified two clusters with significant difference for the two emotional valence conditions: one in the theta/alpha range (5–10 Hz) at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms, Figure 3D, E) after stimulus presentation and another in the theta range (4–7 Hz) at a longer latency (from 2700 to 3300 ms, Figure 3D, F), with higher increase in the identified frequency bands with negative stimuli compared to positive stimuli in both clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation tests on LFP power spectra.

claim: The power of the activity at the identified frequency band for the neutral condition sits between the values for the negative condition and positive condition in both identified time windows.
source: The power of the activity at the identified frequency band for the neutral condition sits between the values for the negative condition and positive condition in both identified time windows (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: There was no significant difference in ERP latency or amplitude caused by different emotional valence stimuli in the habenula.
source: There was no significant difference in ERP latency or amplitude caused by different emotional valence stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of event-related potentials shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The emotional valence effect in the LFP signal is more likely to be driven by non-phase-locked (induced only) activity.
source: These additional analyses demonstrated that the emotional valence effect in the LFP signal is more likely to be driven by non-phase-locked (induced only) activity, even though the possibility of the contribution from transient evoked potentials still cannot be completed excluded.
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analysis removing ERP from time series before frequency-time decomposition.

claim: Permutation test applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects identified clusters with significant differences in the theta/alpha range at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms after stimulus onset) in frontal MEG sensors.
source: Permutation test applied to the power spectra in response to the negative and positive emotional pictures from all subjects identified clusters with significant differences (pcluster < 0.05) in the theta/alpha range at short latency (from 100 to 500 ms after stimulus onset) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation tests on MEG power spectra.

claim: Cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of power changes over the identified frequency band (5–10 Hz) and time window (100–500 ms) confirmed significantly increased activity with negative stimuli in frontal sensors only.
source: Subsequent cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of power changes over the identified frequency band (5–10 Hz) and time window (100–500 ms) confirmed significantly increased activity with negative stimuli in frontal sensors only (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of MEG data.

claim: One main significant source peak of the difference in MEG theta/alpha reactivity was found in the right prefrontal cortex (corresponding to Brodmann area 10, right superior frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [16, 56, 0]).
source: We found two main significant source peaks with one in the right prefrontal cortex (PFC) (corresponding to Brodmann area 10, right superior frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [16, 56, 0]; t-value = 4.14, p=0.046, corrected) (Figure 5A), and the other in the left PFC (corresponding to Brodmann area 9, left middle frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [−32, 38, 28]; t-value = 3.21, p=0.046, corrected) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by frequency-domain beamforming source localization of MEG data.

claim: One main significant source peak of the difference in MEG theta/alpha reactivity was found in the left PFC (corresponding to Brodmann area 9, left middle frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [−32, 38, 28]).
source: We found two main significant source peaks with one in the right prefrontal cortex (PFC) (corresponding to Brodmann area 10, right superior frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [16, 56, 0]; t-value = 4.14, p=0.046, corrected) (Figure 5A), and the other in the left PFC (corresponding to Brodmann area 9, left middle frontal gyrus, MNI coordinate [−32, 38, 28]; t-value = 3.21, p=0.046, corrected) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by frequency-domain beamforming source localization of MEG data.

claim: Comparing the time-varying cortical-habenula coherence for the negative and positive emotional valence conditions showed increased coherence with negative stimulus in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) in the time window of 800–1300 ms.
source: Comparing the time-varying cortical-habenula coherence for the negative and positive emotional valence conditions across all recorded habenula (N = 16 from eight subjects with MEG recordings) showed increased coherence with negative stimulus in the theta/alpha band (5–10 Hz) in the time window of 800–1300 ms (paired t-test, df = 15, p<0.05, uncorrected, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by coherence analysis between LFP and MEG data.

claim: Non-parametric cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of the coherence changes in the 5-10 Hz frequency band and 800–1300 ms time window revealed significantly increased coherence with negative stimuli over right frontal and temporal areas.
source: Subsequent non-parametric cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of the coherence changes in this frequency band and selected time window (800–1300 ms) across the scalp revealed significantly increased coherence with negative stimuli over right frontal and temporal areas (N = 16, Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation statistical analysis of coherence data.

claim: Linear mixed-effect modeling confirmed significant effect of the increase in the theta/alpha band PFC-habenular coherence (relative to the pre-stimulus baseline) during 800–1300 ms on the theta power increase in the habenula at 2700–3300 ms after stimuli onset.
source: Linear mixed-effect modeling confirmed significant effect of the increase in the theta/alpha band PFC-habenular coherence (relative to the pre-stimulus baseline) during this time window (800–1300 ms) on the theta power increase in the habenula at the later time window (2700–3300 ms after stimuli onset) (k = 0.2434 ± 0.1031 (95% confidence interval [0.0358 0.4509]), p=0.0226, R2 = 0.104; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling of the relationship between coherence and power.

claim: Source localization of the theta/alpha habenula-cortical coherence difference for negative and positive stimuli revealed that theta/alpha coherence was higher with negative stimuli in right frontal regions, with the peak t-statistic corresponding to MNI coordinate [10, 64, 12] in the right medial PFC.
source: Source localization of the theta/alpha habenula-cortical coherence difference for negative and positive stimuli revealed that theta/alpha coherence was higher with negative stimuli in right frontal regions, indicated in Figure 6D. The location of the peak t-statistic (t-value = 5.73, p=0.001, uncorrected) corresponds to MNI coordinate [10, 64, 12] and the region encompasses right medial PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by source localization analysis of coherence data.

claim: The models identified significant fixed effects of valence on all the reported changes in the PFC-habenula network.
source: The models identified significant fixed effects of valence on all the reported changes in the PFC-habenula network, but there was no effect of arousal (Table 2 for the modeling and results).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling results presented in Table 2.

claim: The models identified no effect of arousal on the reported changes in the PFC-habenula network.
source: The models identified significant fixed effects of valence on all the reported changes in the PFC-habenula network, but there was no effect of arousal (Table 2 for the modeling and results).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling results presented in Table 2.

claim: The lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the theta/alpha increase within the habenula.
source: The negative effects of valence indicate that the lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the theta/alpha increase within the habenula, the PFC, and in the PFC-habenula theta band coherence, as shown in Figure 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling showing negative effects of valence.

claim: The lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the theta/alpha increase within the PFC.
source: The negative effects of valence indicate that the lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the theta/alpha increase within the habenula, the PFC, and in the PFC-habenula theta band coherence, as shown in Figure 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling showing negative effects of valence.

claim: The lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the increase in the PFC-habenula theta band coherence.
source: The negative effects of valence indicate that the lower the emotional valence score (more negative) of the presented stimuli, the higher the theta/alpha increase within the habenula, the PFC, and in the PFC-habenula theta band coherence, as shown in Figure 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effect modeling showing negative effects of valence.

claim: This is the first study, to our knowledge, implicating increased theta band activities in the habenula-PFC network in negative emotions in human patients.
source: This is the first study, to our knowledge, implicating increased theta band activities in the habenula-PFC network in negative emotions in human patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The LHb has shown consistent hyperactivity in multiple animal models of depression-like phenotypes.
source: The LHb has shown consistent hyperactivity in multiple animal models of depression-like phenotypes (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increased LHb activities have been observed during omission of a predicted reward, depressive-like phenotype, fear or stress.
source: Increased LHb activities have been observed during omission of a predicted reward, depressive-like phenotype, fear or stress (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2011; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Manipulations enhancing or suppressing LHb activity in rodents lead to depressive-like or antidepressant effects, respectively.
source: Furthermore, manipulations enhancing or suppressing LHb activity in rodents lead to depressive-like or antidepressant effects, respectively (Li et al., 2013; Lecca et al., 2016; Cui et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Increased activation of the LHb inhibits dopamine neurons.
source: Increased activation of the LHb inhibits dopamine neurons (Ji and Shepard, 2007; Hikosaka, 2010) and allows avoidance of threatening or unpleasant confrontations (Shumake et al., 2010; Friedman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased activation of the LHb allows avoidance of threatening or unpleasant confrontations.
source: Increased activation of the LHb inhibits dopamine neurons (Ji and Shepard, 2007; Hikosaka, 2010) and allows avoidance of threatening or unpleasant confrontations (Shumake et al., 2010; Friedman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several studies have provided evidence for habenula hyperactivity in human subjects with depressive disorders.
source: In accordance with findings in animal models, several studies have provided evidence for habenula hyperactivity in human subjects with depressive disorders (Morris et al., 1999; Lawson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Ketamine reversed both the increase in theta activity in the habenula and depressive-like behavior in rodents.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that LHb neurons in rodents in the depressive-like state showed increased firing with a mean firing rate in the theta frequency band (Li et al., 2011), and that ketamine reversed both the increase in theta activity in the habenula and depressive-like behavior in rodents (Yang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent study.

claim: Acute 5 Hz DBS of the LHb is associated with depressive-like behavior such as increased duration of immobility in a forced swim test in rodents.
source: The results in this study are also consistent with recent research showing that acute 5 Hz DBS of the LHb is associated with depressive-like behavior such as increased duration of immobility in a forced swim test in rodents (Jakobs et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent DBS study.

claim: LHb receives input from cortical areas processing information about pain, loss, adversities, bad, harmful, or suboptimal choices, such as the anterior insula and dorsal ACC (dACC) and the pregenual ACC (pgACC).
source: Previous studies have showed that LHb receives input from cortical areas processing information about pain, loss, adversities, bad, harmful, or suboptimal choices, such as the anterior insula and dorsal ACC (dACC) and the pregenual ACC (pgACC) (Vadovičová, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PFC-to-habenular projections provide a teaching signal for value-based choice behavior, helping to learn to avoid potentially harmful, low-valued or wrong choices.
source: Our data is consistent with the hypothesis that PFC-to-habenular projections provide a teaching signal for value-based choice behavior, helping to learn to avoid potentially harmful, low-valued or wrong choices (Vadovičová, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: The Right Hemisphere Hypothesis (RHH) suggests that the right hemisphere would be involved, more than the left hemisphere, in the processing of all emotional stimuli, irrespective of their emotional valence.
source: The Right Hemisphere Hypothesis (RHH) suggests that the right hemisphere would be involved, more than the left hemisphere, in the processing of all emotional stimuli, irrespective of their emotional valence (Gainotti, 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: The Valence Hypothesis (VH) posits that the left and the right hemispheres would be specialized in processing positive and negative emotions, respectively.
source: On the other hand, the Valence Hypothesis (VH) posits that the left and the right hemispheres would be specialized in processing positive and negative emotions, respectively (Davidson, 1992; Wyczesany et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: The Valence Hypothesis has been supported by studies of brain lesion, electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and functional neuroimaging in the PFC.
source: The latter hypothesis has also been supported by studies of brain lesion (Starkstein et al., 1987; Morris et al., 1999), electroencephalography (EEG) (Davidson, 1992; Wyczesany et al., 2018), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) (Pascual-Leone et al., 1996), and functional neuroimaging (Canli et al., 1998; Beraha et al., 2012) in the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple types of studies.

claim: High-frequency DBS delivered to STN and GPi can reduce the firing rates of local neurons.
source: Although the exact underlying physiological mechanism of DBS remains elusive, high-frequency DBS delivered to STN and GPi can reduce the firing rates of local neurons (Boraud et al., 1996; Welter et al., 2004) and suppress the hypersynchrony of oscillatory activities in the beta frequency band in the network, leading to symptom alleviation (Kuhn et al., 2008; Oswal et al., 2016) for Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-frequency DBS delivered to STN and GPi can suppress the hypersynchrony of oscillatory activities in the beta frequency band in the network, leading to symptom alleviation for Parkinson's disease.
source: Although the exact underlying physiological mechanism of DBS remains elusive, high-frequency DBS delivered to STN and GPi can reduce the firing rates of local neurons (Boraud et al., 1996; Welter et al., 2004) and suppress the hypersynchrony of oscillatory activities in the beta frequency band in the network, leading to symptom alleviation (Kuhn et al., 2008; Oswal et al., 2016) for Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-frequency DBS may dissociate input and output signals, resulting in the disruption of abnormal information flow through the stimulation site.
source: In addition, high-frequency DBS may also dissociate input and output signals, resulting in the disruption of abnormal information flow through the stimulation site (Chiken and Nambu, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for Parkinson's disease.
source: This is supported by recent studies showing that patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for Parkinson's disease (Horn et al., 2017), major depressive disorder (MDD) (Riva-Posse et al., 2014), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Baldermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for major depressive disorder (MDD).
source: This is supported by recent studies showing that patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for Parkinson's disease (Horn et al., 2017), major depressive disorder (MDD) (Riva-Posse et al., 2014), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Baldermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
source: This is supported by recent studies showing that patient-specific connectivity profiles between the stimulation target and area of interest in the cortex can predict clinical outcome of DBS for Parkinson's disease (Horn et al., 2017), major depressive disorder (MDD) (Riva-Posse et al., 2014), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Baldermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High-frequency DBS targeting habenula may be beneficial for treatment-resistant MDD by inhibiting possible hyperactivity and theta band over-synchrony of neuronal activities in the habenula.
source: High-frequency DBS targeting habenula may be beneficial for treatment-resistant MDD by inhibiting possible hyperactivity and theta band over-synchrony of neuronal activities in the habenula and by disrupting the information flow from the PFC to other midbrain areas through the habenula.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the study's findings and prior knowledge about DBS mechanisms.

claim: High-frequency DBS targeting habenula may be beneficial for treatment-resistant MDD by disrupting the information flow from the PFC to other midbrain areas through the habenula.
source: High-frequency DBS targeting habenula may be beneficial for treatment-resistant MDD by inhibiting possible hyperactivity and theta band over-synchrony of neuronal activities in the habenula and by disrupting the information flow from the PFC to other midbrain areas through the habenula.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the study's findings and prior knowledge about DBS mechanisms.

claim: Theta band synchronization can potentially be used as a biomarker for closed loop habenula DBS for better treatment of MDD.
source: It remains to be explored whether theta band synchronization can be used as a biomarker for closed loop habenula DBS for better treatment of MDD.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: The response to emotional tasks is likely to be altered in patients with pathological mood states compared to healthy subjects.
source: The response to emotional tasks is likely to be altered in patients with pathological mood states compared to healthy subjects.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study based on general knowledge.

claim: The human habenula has a combined volume (sum of left and right hemispheres) of approximately 30–36 mm³.
